facts.text: The only hitter of the 1930s to score 120 runs with 50 RBI or fewer: Frankie Crosetti, 1937 — 127 R, 49 RBI.
The only pitcher of the 1930s to strike out 150 and win 10 games or fewer: Bob Feller, 1937 — 150 K, 9-7.
The only hitter of the 1930s to bat .300 with 30 homers, 100 RBI and 20 steals: Chuck Klein, 1932 — .348, 38 HR, 137 RBI, 20 SB.
The only hitter of the 1930s to ground into 28+ double plays: Ernie Lombardi, 1938 — 30 GIDP.
The only hitter of the 1930s to hit 30+ homers with 15 doubles or fewer: Babe Ruth, 1932 — 41 HR, 13 2B.
The only hitter of the 1930s to bat .400 (400+ PA): Bill Terry, 1930 — .401.

Just four hitters of the 1930s drew 100 walks and struck out 100 times: Jimmie Foxx (1936, 105 BB, 119 K); Dolph Camilli (1938, 119 BB, 101 K); Dolph Camilli (1939, 110 BB, 107 K); Hank Greenberg (1937, 102 BB, 101 K).
Jimmie Foxx hit 25+ home runs in 10 straight seasons (1930-39), the longest run of the 1930s.
Lou Gehrig batted .300 or better (500+ PA) in 8 straight seasons (1930-37), the longest run of the 1930s.
Only two hitters of the 1930s drew more walks than hits (400+ PA): Max Bishop (1930, 128 BB, 111 H); Max Bishop (1932, 110 BB, 104 H).
Only two pitchers of the 1930s won 15 games walking 30 batters or fewer: Red Lucas (1936, 15-4, 26 BB); Ray Brown (1938, 15-0, 29 BB).
Only two pitchers of the 1930s threw 8+ shutouts: Carl Hubbell (1933, 10 SHO); Bill Lee (1938, 9 SHO).
Just three hitters of the 1930s hit 25+ homers at age 36 or older: Babe Ruth (1931, 46 HR at 36); Babe Ruth (1932, 41 HR at 37); Babe Ruth (1933, 34 HR at 38).
Only two pitchers of the 1930s posted an ERA under 2.00 (162+ IP): Slim Jones (1934, 1.60 ERA in 203.0 IP); Carl Hubbell (1933, 1.66 ERA in 308.2 IP).
Only two hitters of the 1930s batted .310 while slugging under .380 (500+ PA): Luke Appling (1939, .314 AVG, .368 SLG); Dick Bartell (1934, .310 AVG, .373 SLG).
Charlie Gehringer collected 200+ hits in 5 straight seasons (1933-37), the longest run of the 1930s.
Lou Gehrig drew 100+ walks in 5 straight seasons (1934-38), the longest run of the 1930s.
Dizzy Dean struck out 150+ in 5 straight seasons (1932-36), the longest run of the 1930s.

Just four hitters of the 1930s batted .320 or better with 20 walks or fewer (500+ PA): Gee Walker (1932, .323, 13 BB); Woody Jensen (1935, .324, 15 BB); Carl Reynolds (1930, .359, 20 BB); Frank McCormick (1938, .327, 18 BB).
19 times in the 1930s a hitter played a full season without a single home run (600+ PA). The most extreme: Doc Cramer, 1938 — 0 HR in 717 PA.
14 times in the 1930s a hitter drove in 100 runs with 8 homers or fewer. The most extreme: Luke Appling, 1936 — 128 RBI, 6 HR.
6 times in the 1930s a hitter collected 230 hits. The most extreme: Bill Terry, 1930 — 254 H.
21 times in the 1930s a hitter drove in 150 runs. The most extreme: Hack Wilson, 1930 — 191 RBI.
17 times in the 1930s a pitcher threw 300 innings. The most extreme: Bobo Newsom, 1938 — 329.2 IP.
14 times in the 1930s a pitcher walked 130+ batters. The most extreme: Bob Feller, 1938 — 208 BB.
Most steals by a 30-homer hitter of the 1930s: Chuck Klein, 1932 — 20 SB with 38 HR.
Most home runs per RBI of the 1930s: Hank Greenberg, 1938 — 58 HR but only 146 RBI.
Fewest strikeouts by a 25-homer hitter of the 1930s: Joe DiMaggio, 1939 — 20 K with 30 HR.
Highest average by a hitter with 3 homers or fewer: Paul Waner, 1937 — .354 with 2 HR.
Most walks by a sub-.240 hitter of the 1930s: Frankie Crosetti, 1937 — 86 BB while batting .234.
Most RBI per home run among 100-RBI seasons: Pie Traynor, 1931 — 103 RBI on 2 HR.
Most wins by a pitcher with an ERA over 5.00: Ray Kremer, 1930 — 20-12 with a 5.02 ERA.
Fewest wins by a qualified pitcher with an ERA under 3.00: Steve Swetonic, 1932 — 11-6 despite a 2.82 ERA.
Most strikeouts by a pitcher with a losing record: Van Mungo, 1936 — 238 K, 18-19.
Most losses by a pitcher with an ERA under 3.50: Paul Derringer, 1933 — 7-27 with a 3.30 ERA.
Fewest strikeouts by a 20-game winner of the 1930s: Ben Cantwell, 1933 — 57 K, 20-10.
Most innings in a season without a complete game: Jim Bivin, 1935 — 161.2 IP, 0 CG.
Most home runs allowed in a season this decade: Lon Warneke, 1937 — 32 HR allowed, 18-11.
8 hitter-seasons of the 1930s ended on a .299 average, one point short of .300 — among them Earl Averill Sr. (1937), Goose Goslin (1932), Bob Johnson (1935).
18 pitcher-seasons of the 1930s ended on exactly 19 wins, one short of 20 — among them Heinie Meine (1931), Paul Derringer (1936), Bill Lee (1939).
9 teams of the 1930s won 100 games; the best record was the 1931 Athletics at 107-45.
Youngest player of the 1930s to hit 25 home runs: Ted Williams, age 20 in 1939 — 31 HR.
Youngest player of the 1930s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Mel Ott, age 21 in 1930 — .349.
Oldest player of the 1930s to bat .330 (500+ PA): Sam Rice, age 40 in 1930 — .349.
Youngest player of the 1930s to drive in 100 runs: Ted Williams, age 20 in 1939 — 145 RBI.
Youngest player of the 1930s to steal 30 bases: Ben Chapman, age 22 in 1931 — 61 SB.
Oldest player of the 1930s to steal 30 bases: Kiki Cuyler, age 31 in 1930 — 37 SB.
Oldest player of the 1930s to win 20 games: Ray Kremer, age 37 in 1930 — 20-12.
Oldest player of the 1930s to strike out 150: Dazzy Vance, age 40 in 1931 — 150 K.
Youngest player of the 1930s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Slim Jones, age 21 in 1934 — 1.60 ERA.
Oldest player of the 1930s to post a qualified ERA under 2.75: Dazzy Vance, age 39 in 1930 — 2.61 ERA.
13 teams of the 1930s had two players at 30+ home runs; the biggest pairing was the 1930 Chicago Cubs — Hack Wilson 56, Gabby Hartnett 37.
20 teams of the 1930s had two players at 200+ hits; the biggest pairing was the 1937 Detroit Tigers — Gee Walker 213, Charlie Gehringer 209, Pete Fox 208.
12 teams of the 1930s had two players at 20 wins; the biggest pairing was the 1931 Philadelphia Athletics — Lefty Grove 31, George Earnshaw 21, Rube Walberg 20.
5 teams of the 1930s had two players at 150+ strikeouts; the biggest pairing was the 1930 Philadelphia Athletics — Lefty Grove 209, George Earnshaw 193.
Most home runs in the 1930s by a hitter who never led the majors in a season: Mel Ott, 308.
Most hits of the 1930s: Paul Waner, 1959.
Most stolen bases of the 1930s: Ben Chapman, 269.
Most triples of the 1930s: Earl Averill Sr., 114.
Most strikeouts of the 1930s: Lefty Gomez, 1337.
Most complete games of the 1930s: Wes Ferrell, 207.
Most walks issued in the 1930s: Bump Hadley, 1061.
1937 had 14 25-homer hitters, the most of any season in the 1930s.
1933 had just 5 25-homer hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1930s.
1930 had 60 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the most of any season in the 1930s.
1933 had just 34 .300 hitters (500+ PA), the fewest of any season in the 1930s.
1930 had 33 100-RBI hitters, the most of any season in the 1930s.
1933 had just 12 100-RBI hitters, the fewest of any season in the 1930s.
1937 had 3 30-steal players, the most of any season in the 1930s.
1933 had no 30-steal players at all — one of the seasons of the 1930s without one.
1930 had 20 200-hit seasons, the most of any season in the 1930s.
1938 had just 2 200-hit seasons, the fewest of any season in the 1930s.
1934 had 9 20-game winners, the most of any season in the 1930s.
1938 had just 4 20-game winners, the fewest of any season in the 1930s.
11 teams of the 1930s lost 100 games; the worst was the 1935 Braves at 38-115.
Best run differential of the 1930s: the 1939 Yankees, +411 (967 scored, 556 allowed).
8 times in the 1930s a hitter batted .320 at age 36 or older (500+ PA). The most extreme: Sam Rice, 1930 — .349 at 40.
3 hitter-seasons of the 1930s ended on exactly 99 RBI, one short of 100 — among them George Grantham (1930), Pinky Higgins (1933), Arky Vaughan (1935).
9 times in the 1930s a hitter hit 45 doubles and 5 homers or fewer. The most extreme: Billy Herman, 1936 — 57 2B, 5 HR.
Exactly one pitcher of the 1930s finished a season with exactly 199 strikeouts, one short of 200: Dizzy Dean (1933).
Worst run differential of the 1930s: the 1932 Red Sox, -349 (566 scored, 915 allowed).
6 times in the 1930s a pitcher won 20 and lost 15 in the same season. The most extreme: Alvin Crowder, 1933 — 24-15.
26 times in the 1930s a pitcher completed 25+ games. The most extreme: Wes Ferrell, 1935 — 31 CG.
7 times in the 1930s a pitcher won 20 games with an ERA of 4.00 or worse. The most extreme: Lefty Gomez, 1932 — 24-7, 4.21 ERA.
9 times in the 1930s a hitter hit 25+ homers at age 22 or younger. The most extreme: Joe DiMaggio, 1937 — 46 HR at 22.
83 times in the 1930s a hitter hit 12+ triples and more triples than homers. The most extreme: John Stone, 1935 — 18 3B, 1 HR.
7 times in the 1930s a hitter got hit by 12+ pitches. The most extreme: Ival Goodman, 1938 — 15 HBP.

method: Every fact is a predicate evaluated over every hitter-season and pitcher-season in the decade, pulled in full from the MLB Stats API (the official record). Nothing is recalled or estimated; the rows that satisfy each rule are stored with it.

'Only', 'two' and 'three/four' claims are exact counts across the complete pull. Where a rule uses a plate-appearance or innings floor instead of a league qualification bar, the floor is stated in the fact so the claim is reproducible.
Thresholds are era-aware (strikeouts, saves and home runs meant different things in 1925 and 1995) and are recorded in the file.
Rules built from plain comparisons carry a Stathead Season Finder spec with the same filters and year range, for independent re-checking on the subscription.
